Learning Objectives
Assess the anatomy and biomechanics of the bony articulations of the knee joint, the primary
ligaments of the knee, and the secondary stabilizers of the knee and their translational
constraints.
Review the anatomy of the extensor mechanism, posterolateral corner, and posteromedial
corner, and determine how groups of structures within these areas work together
biomechanically to provide stability.
Explain the relationship between the patella and trochlea, and examine how trochlear
dysplasia may affect the extensor mechanism.
Assess the structure of the menisci, and evaluate how they are functionally affected by tears
and degeneration.

Introduction

Introduction
As the largest joint in the human body, the knee—its structure and mechanics—
commands the attention of orthopaedic surgeons, emergency physicians, family practice
physicians, physical therapists, and any healthcare professional who has a healthy
interest in the extremities. For sports medicine surgeons, a comprehensive
understanding of every level of the composition of the knee is essential, from the
vascular structure and collagen fiber orientation in the menisci to the gross landmarks
essential for proper orientation and positioning of bone tunnels.
The articulatio genus (the knee joint; not to be confused with the small articularis genus
muscle) is presented in this lesson from various viewpoints, from microscopic to gross
anatomic. The same structure may be represented using schematic, cadaver model,
radiographic, and arthroscopic images. This variety will provide a more complete
perspective of not only the individual components of the joint but also their relationships
to one another and, ultimately, their biomechanical function.
Relationships and landmarks highlighted by current research that may be of particular
relevance to sports medicine surgeons will be highlighted. Joint biomechanics will be
presented with an emphasis on the relevance of surgical correction of ligamentous,
cartilaginous, and meniscal injuries and functional rehabilitation or return to play. In
addition, the anatomic attachments of the important ligaments and tendons will be
described with precise measurements from cadaver model studies, if possible.

Distal Femur
A thorough understanding of the distal end of the femur is essential for sports medicine
surgeons (Figure 1). The contours of the distal femur serve as the attachment points of
numerous muscles, ligaments, and capsular structures, and the shape and orientation of
its articular surfaces determine the mechanics of motion and load distribution
transmitted through the joint. The separate articulations of the medial femoral condyle
with the medial tibial plateau, the lateral femoral condyle with the lateral tibial plateau,
and the femoral trochlea with the articular surface of the patella have been used to
divide the knee joint into three compartments: medial, lateral, and patellofemoral.
The anterior shaft of the distal femur is smooth and free of attachments below the
vastus intermedius origin, apart from that of the tiny articularis genu muscle. The
posterior aspect of the shaft has a long bony ridge, the linea aspera, which serves as an
attachment for the thigh adductors, the short head of the biceps femoris, and an
intramuscular septum. The medial lip of the linea serves as insertion for the adductor
longus, magnus (distal), and brevis (proximal) and provides the origin of the vastus
medialis. The lateral lip of the linea contains the origins of the vastus lateralis, vastus

The distal end of the femur fans out into medial and lateral condyles separated by a
groove covered by articular cartilage called the femoral trochlea, and each condyle hosts
a small epicondyle. On the medial side of the distal femur, three osseous prominences
arise, which are of importance in ligament reconstruction: the medial epicondyle, the
adductor tubercle, and the gastrocnemius tubercle. The mean relationships between
these medial-sided structures have been determined in cadaver model studies.1 The
adductor tubercle, on which the adductor magnus tendon inserts, is 12.6 mm proximal
and 8.3 mm posterior to the medial epicondyle. Occasionally, the adductor magnus
tendon is referred to as the lighthouse of the medial knee because it is a convenient
landmark to locate medial femorla structure attachment sites. The gastrocnemius
tubercle is 9.4 mm distal and 8.7 mm posterior to the adductor tubercle and 13.7 mm
posterior to the medial epicondyle. The medial head of the gastrocnemius originates at
this gastrocnemius tubercle just superior to the joint capsule on the lateral medial
condyle.
The lateral and posterior aspects of the distal femur contain numerous attachment.
According to cadaver model studies, the LGT attaches first to a bony or cartilaginous
fabella (if present) and courses on to attach to a lateral supracondylar process in 80% of
individuals.2 This femoral attachment is a mean of 13.8 mm posterior to the femoral FCL
attachment and 28.3 mm from the PLT attachment.
The slightly larger and more distal medial condyle has a mean sagittal angulation of 22°,3
and continues more distally than the lateral condyle. This difference in length accounts
for the 5° to 7° of physiologic valgus along the femoral anatomic axis in adult knees.4
The trochlear groove deepens into the intercondylar sulcus, which is an important
landmark in determination of trochlear dysplasia, often in patient with recurrent patellar
dislocations. The arch of the intercondylar notch contains the femoral footprints of the
cruciate and meniscofemoral ligaments (MFLs). An osteochondral groove or depression,

Proximal Tibia
The proximal tibia is composed of two mostly flat condyles, termed the medial and
lateral plateaus, a large anterior tubercle, and a balcony-like drop-off posteriorly. The
medial plateau has a very slight concavity, which allows the medial femoral condyle to
rest within the medial tibial plateau; the concavity is deepened by a squared-off
posterior aspect. The medial plateau is more ovoid and distal relative to the lateral
plateau. The lateral plateau is more circular, and its articular surface is flat to slightly
convex. The lateral femoral condyle is relatively more planar, or even convex, whereas
the medial tibial plateau is slightly concave.2,5
On the anterior shaft of the tibia, a large protuberance called the tibial tuberosity serves
as the insertion of the patellar tendon inferiorly. Lateral to medial from the tibial
tuberosity are the broader insertion of the sartorius and the smaller insertions of the
gracilis and semitendinosus. The insertion of these three tendons is known as the pes
anserinus, or the goose foot. The Gerdy tubercle lies lateral and proximal to the tibial
tuberosity, serving as the distal insertion of the ITB.
A coronal plane slope exists from the more superior lateral plateau to the more distal
medial plateau. The coronal plane tibial slope tends to be larger in males; however, the
importance of this anatomy is unclear.6
PTS is an important consideration in cruciate ligament reconstruction. Both plateaus
have a posterior slope, and a smaller lateral tibial plateau is associated with a steeper
slope. A longitudinal 20-year study showed that a PTS greater than 12° is the most
important factor in ACL reinjury, particularly in adolescents.7 Biomechanical studies have
shown that compressive loads across the joint generate anterior and proximal force
components and that the magnitude of the anterior vector increases in direct proportion
to the steepness of PTS.6,8,9 This anteriorly directed force results in increased anterior
tibial translation (ATT), especially in extension.8,9 Increased PTS also generates torque
across the joint.8 Morphologies of tibial slope may vary by sex, with the mean PTS in
females being higher than that in males. This has been suggested as a predisposing

The tibial plateau also contains an intercondylar bony eminence between the medial and

lateral spine. The medial and lateral spines appear adjacent on a coronal view; however,

articular surface with the intercondylar notch in a saddle-like distribution14 (Figure 2).
Posteriorly, the tibial plateau drops onto a ledge at the location at which the PCL
attaches, inferior to the level of the tibial plateau. This down-sloping shelf is known as
the champagne-glass drop-off and is an important landmark in PCL reconstruction. The
fibula articulates with an ovoid articular facet on the posteroinferior aspect of the lateral
tibial condyle.

Tibiofemoral Articulation
The primary bony constituents of the tibiofemoral articulation are the femoral condyles
and the tibial plateaus. The medial femoral condyle sits atop the relatively concave
medial tibial plateau, providing a certain degree of congruence to the medial side of the
knee. The lateral femoral condyle articulates with the relatively flat or convex lateral
tibial plateau, leading to inherent instability in the PLC.2,5 The femur and tibia function as
a hinge joint restrained by a constellation of static and dynamic soft-tissue
stabilizers.14,15 The geometry of this arrangement also leads to a phenomenon called
the screw-home mechanism: the larger and more distal medial femoral condyle glides
across the medial tibial plateau, resulting in relative external rotation of the tibia with
regard to the femur or internal rotation of the femur by approximately 15° during the
last 20° of open-chain (non–weight-bearing) extension.15 During closed-chain extension,
such as during the gait cycle, the femur internally rotates on the planted tibia.15,16 The
net effect is posteriorly directed translational and rotatory stress restrained by the
PCL.17
Varus and valgus alignment are another concern in consideration of the tibiofemoral
articulation; the tibial spines are important landmarks in this determination. A line
drawn from the center of the femoral head to the midpoint of the talar dome on an AP
radiograph should appear to pass between the tibial spines in a neutrally aligned knee. If
the line falls medial to the tibial spines, the leg is in varus alignment, whereas if the line
passes lateral to the tibial spines, the knee is in valgus alignment.18,19 (Figure 3)

Proximal Tibiofibular Joint: Diarthrodial Synovial Joint
The bony anatomy of the fibular head is quite simple; it has a sharp styloid process with
a posteriorly rising apex, which slopes forward to a flat or oblique surface. The knob-like
fibular head articulates with the posterolateral inferior aspect of the lateral tibial condyle
and aids in dynamic and static restraint of the knee by providing attachment sites for the
biceps femoris, FCL, popliteofibular ligament (PFL), and many other structures. Beneath
the head, the fibula narrows into a neck region and is attached longitudinally along its
medial facet to the tibia via the interosseous membrane. The common peroneal nerve
descends close to the posterior aspect of the fibular head, between the biceps femoris
tendon and the lateral gastrocnemius, and winds anteriorly around the fibular neck. This

The proximal tibiofibular joint (PTFJ) is a diarthrodial joint lined with synovial membrane,
with a capsule reinforced by tibiofibular ligaments. Ogden20 found that the PTFJ is highly
variable in the contours of its articular surface between individuals because of a wide
range of obliquities of the fibular head as it slopes anteroinferiorly from the fibular
styloid. These different shapes of the fibular head lead to varying degrees of slight
convexity, concavity, or co-planarity of the articular surfaces, which may predispose
some patients to instability. The chief intrinsic restraints of this joint are the more
superior and proximal posterior tibiofibular ligament and the anterior tibiofibular
ligament. Symptomatic injury typically involves anterolateral subluxation of the fibular
head and leads to irritation of the common peroneal nerve at the location at which it
crosses the proximal fibula.
The PTFJ allows for a small degree of motion of the fibular head relative to the proximal
tibia. Dorsiflexion at the ankle causes external rotation of the fibular head, with
increased dorsiflexion leading to a higher degree of external rotation. The attachments
of the FCL and the short head of the biceps femoris may account for the behavior of the
joint in flexion and extension. The FCL tightens in extension and relaxes at
approximately 30° of flexion. Relaxation of the FCL allows for more tibial rotation and
anteroposterior fibular head motion. In flexion, relative laxity of the FCL and the biceps
femoris allows for more anterior motion of the fibular head; whereas in extension, the
FCL is taut, and the biceps tendon exerts more tension, pulling the fibular head more
posteriorly.20 Isometric reconstruction techniques have been developed to restore
stability across the PTFJ for acute and chronic injuries.2 Rajan et al21 presented a
systematic review on and 10-year experience with proximal tibiofibular joint dislocations,
reporting an association between severe proximal tibiofibular injuries and potential
amputation.

Patellofemoral Joint
The patellofemoral joint consists of the articulation between the patella and the distal
femoral trochlea. Joint congruence during movement of the patella along the trochlea is
affected by various forces and discreet structures; therefore, problems with the
patellofemoral joint frequently are encountered in orthopaedic practice.22-26 The static
restraints provided by articular surfaces, as well as active muscular tension and the
influence of retinacular structures, guide normal patellofemoral joint mechanics.
Patellofemoral Articular Surfaces
The patella is the largest sesamoid bone in the human body and has seven different articular
facets. This surface geometry of the patella contributes to appropriate tracking as it slides within
the trochlear groove, with the posterior bony surfaces of the patella serving as static restraints.
The medial and lateral trochlear facets, located superiorly in relation to the trochlear groove, also
serve as static restraints against patellar maltracking. The larger lateral femoral condyle is more

Soft-tissue structures between the skin and joint provide passive or static restraints to
patellar instability during motion along the trochlear groove.36 Among these, the MPFL
has been reported to account for approximately one-half of the total restraint to lateral
patellar displacement.37-42 Although information about the femoral origin of the MPFL
varies in the literature, it has been consistently identified between the adductor tubercle
and the medial epicondyle.37,38,43 In a more quantitative study, the femoral origin of the
MPFL was reported to be 9.6 mm anterodistal to the adductor tubercle and 15.2 mm
proximal and posterior to the medial epicondyle.44 The mean length of the MPFL ranges
from 53 mm to 55 mm, and the width of the MPFL may vary from 3 mm to 30 mm,
widening at its attachments.40,45
Rupture of the medial passive patellar restraints causes lateral translation and increased
lateral trochlear contact pressure. This effect is particularly observable early in flexion.
The greatest change in MPFL strain has been reported to occur in the first 30° of
flexion.46 Past 60° of flexion, lateral patellar translation generally is prevented by
trochlear curvature, and the force required to dislocate the patella is independent of the
integrity of medial passive patellar restraints.46
Although the MPFL is the primary passive restraint to lateral patellofemoral translation,
new evidence suggests that the MPTL, MPML, and MQTFL also play important roles in
medial patellar stability37,47 (Figure 5). Among these, the MQTFL stems from the same
femoral origin as the MPFL and courses proximally toward the quadriceps tendon, at
which it is termed a proximal medial patellar restraint along with the MPFL. Conversely,

Patellar Tracking
The patella moves in the medial-lateral direction and does not enter the trochlear groove
if the knee is in extension and the quadriceps muscle is relaxed. In early flexion, the
patella moves medially because of the summed vectors of muscles pulling and the
orientation of the patellar tendon and the medial and lateral retinacular structures;
however, preserving the appropriate course of patellar tracking at higher flexion angles
is more dependent on the trochlear curvature. With the knee in extension, the patella
moves proximally and slightly laterally during initial contraction of the quadriceps
muscle. At this point, lateral movement of the patella is balanced by tension of the
medial patellar retinacular structures. If knee flexion is maintained, stability is provided
by the patella engaging with the trochlea as a result of increased patellofemoral joint
force from quadriceps tension.33
During knee flexion, contact areas in the trochlea and patella and the pressures acting
thereon vary with different angles of flexion. The lateral facet of the patella has a higher
contribution to the total contact area compared with the medial facet because of the
effect of the Q angle.59 On the femoral side, with as much as 90° of flexion, the contact
area in the trochlea tends to shift from the lateral to the medial and then back to the
lateral facet.60 With additional flexion, the contact area is more evenly distributed
between the two femoral condyles if the patella reaches the intercondylar notch.53
During flexion, the combination of vectors created by the patellar tendon and the
quadriceps acting in opposing sagittal directions generate a posteriorly oriented force on
the patella.
Superior-inferior positioning of the patella also is an important influence on the joint and
its stability. A high-riding patella (ie, patella alta) poses a risk to stability because it causes
delayed engagement of the patella to the trochlea. A low-riding patella (ie, patella baja)

The Menisci
The medial and lateral menisci are fibrocartilaginous, wedge-shaped structures that
form asymmetric cushions across the tibiofemoral joint and, together, are integral to the
normal transmission of forces across the knee. The menisci improve joint congruency
and increase the contact area between the femoral condyles and the tibial plateau,
reducing peak contact pressures and protecting the articular cartilage.70-72 The menisci
are primarily composed of water, proteoglycans, and type I collagen fibers arranged in
longitudinal and radial orientations.
The microscopic anatomy of the meniscus is complex, with circumferential and radially
oriented collagen fibers. The longitudinal fibers convert axial loading forces into
circumferential hoop stresses, which allows the meniscus to dissipate forces across the
joint and minimize contact stresses between articular cartilage surfaces.71,73 Firm
anchor points posteriorly and anteriorly to the tibia, along with attachments to the joint
capsule and the surrounding ligaments and tendons, prevent meniscal extrusion. A tear
in one of the meniscal roots is functionally equivalent to a meniscectomy because
severance from one of its anchor points causes the meniscus to extrude and lose its
cushioning and pressure-dissipating qualities.70,74 Biomechanical studies have shown a
decrease in contact area of 50% to 70% and drastically increased peak contact pressures
(as high as 300%) after meniscectomy.71,73,75-79 These changes may lead to the rapid
onset of osteoarthritis and joint space narrowing and are associated with a high rate of
conversion to arthroplasty80 (Figure 12). Classic post-meniscectomy changes to the
knee, including “squaring of the femoral condyles, joint space narrowing, and ridge
formation,” were reported by Fairbank in 1948. These effects also are observed with
radial and root tears, which disrupt the circumferential fibers and result in a similar
functional deficit.81

The cruciate ligaments are incredibly tough structures with a unique microanatomic makeup. The
ACL will be used to illustrate these properties given the abundant research available. In the ACL,

collagenous matrix and forms parallel fibril bundles that give the ACL most of its tensile strength.

type II collagen, which more often is found in cartilage, has been observed in the bony
attachment sites of the cruciate ligaments and may act to resist shear force. Water, mostly

Anterior Cruciate Ligament
Although the ACL was first described in 1836 by Weber and Weber,105 its precise
anatomic attachments were confirmed in the last decade of the 20th century.106 Grossly,
the ACL runs from the lateral aspect of the femoral intercondylar notch to the anterior
part of the tibial intercondylar eminence. The femoral origin at its largest cross-sectional
area is 20 mm long and 10 mm wide, and the tibial insertion is slightly larger at 30 mm
long by 10 mm wide at its greatest extent.104,107 The center of the ACL femoral origin
(Figure 15) is at the level of the adductor tubercle if a horizontal line is drawn from the
adductor tubercle through the intercondylar notch in the sagittal plane. The origin of the
ACL is horizontal if the knee is in 90° of flexion and vertical in extension.104
Wide variability exists in the size of not only the ACL and its attachment sites but also the
morphology of the intercondylar notch and the distal femur;3,107 however, consistent
relationships between ACL attachment sites are observed and are essential for anatomic
reconstruction. A series of bony landmarks that serve to identify the femoral and tibial
attachments for the two ACL bundles has been described.108 On the femur, two ridges
and two points that outline the oval footprints of each bundle have been described. The
lateral intercondylar ridge, traditionally known as the resident ridge, extends a mean of
18 mm along the lateral wall of the intercondylar notch and is anterior to the footprints
of the AMB and PLB.106,108,109 Perpendicular to the lateral intercondylar ridge, the
bifurcate ridge extends a mean of 11.6 mm from the midpoint of the lateral
intercondylar ridge to the edge of the lateral condylar articular cartilage. The bifurcate
ridge divides the footprint of the AMB from that of the PLB, the centers of which are
approximately 10 mm apart. The proximal point is a point at the apex of the proximal
curvature of the articular cartilage. The posterior point is the posterior-most point along
the margin of the lateral condylar articular cartilage.108 These landmarks serve as
guideposts for anatomic reconstruction of the ACL (Figures 16-18).

The MCL is one of the most often injured structures in the knee126 and is part of a

forms much of the floor of the pes anserine bursa, posteriorly blending with distal
expansions of the semimembranosus tendon. The inferior medial geniculate artery and

Lateral-Sided Structures and the PLC
Traditionally, lateral-sided structures and the PLC were not well understood, which
almost always led to poor outcomes after repair. Biomechanical studies and clinical data
have demonstrated a high rate of success if all structures are reconstructed via
appropriately oriented femoral, tibial, and fibular tunnels. To understand these
reconstruction techniques, which involve the use multiple grafts and tunnels in close
association, a concrete understanding of lateral-sided structures and the PLC—one of
the most complex areas in the lower extremity with 28 associated structures2 is
required. Traditionally, the lateral aspect of the knee was described in three layers: layer
1 contains superficial fascia (or fascia lata), biceps femoris, and iliotibial tract; layer 2
contains the lateral retinaculum of the quadriceps tendon and the patellofemoral
ligaments; and layer 3 is capsular.3 The authors of this lesson feel that descriptions of
the individual structures and their biomechanical roles is more important than their
arrangement in layers, especially because anatomic studies increasingly indicate more
complicated relationships and extensive connections to bone than previously suspected.

In recent decades, interest in the ITB has increased because of its contribution to
restraint of internal rotation, especially in consideration of residual anterolateral laxity
after ACL reconstruction. The ITB originates as a fascial thickening from the tensor fascia
lata muscle, originating at the iliac crest and travelling down the distal femur. The deep
aspect of the ITB attaches to the distal femur via two fibrous bundles known as the
proximal and distal Kaplan fibers. The proximal bundle courses transversely from the
superficial ITB to attach to a bony landmark, termed the proximal ridge, inferior to the
intermuscular septum and 53.6 mm proximal to the lateral epicondyle.162 The distal
bundle of Kaplan fibers courses more distally and medially, attaching to a distal ridge on
the femur, approximately 31.4 mm proximal to the lateral femoral epicondyle (Figure
26). The distal bundle quite strong, with a maximum load at failure of 170.2 N, which is
only slightly less than the maximum load of failure of the ALL (175 N).162 The superficial
ITB has a large attachment to the Gerdy tubercle on the anterolateral tibia
(approximately 430 mm2) but also extends in a more complicated web of connections. A
deeper fascial component of the distal ITB, known as the capsulo-osseous layer, forms
another connection between the distal femur (attaching just proximal to the LGT on the
distal ridge) and the proximal tibia (attaching at the lateral tibial tuberosity, just
posteromedial to the Gerdy tubercle).147,162-164 The proximal capsulo-osseous layer also
gives contributions to the fascia surrounding the LGT and the short head of the biceps
femoris.162 Finally, an anterior expansion of the ITB, known as the iliopatellar band,
inserts into the lateral aspects of the patella and the patellar tendon162 and, through this
connection the ITB, plays a role in patellar tracking.139

The synovial plica is a substantial embryologic remnant that may cause problems in
adults. It has been reported in 95% of patients during arthroscopy;165 however, its
development is highly variable between individuals. The plica consists of an intra-

limited superiorly by the inferior pole of the patella, posterosuperiorly by the synovium

The prepatellar bursa is a large, subcutaneous structure that can become inflamed with

patellar tendon on the tibial tuberosity, inferior to the retropatellar fat pad, and does not
communicate with the knee joint.169

Innervation
Innervation to the lower limb proceeds chiefly from the sciatic (L4 through S3), femoral
(L2 through L4), and obturator (L2 through L4) nerves. The sciatic nerve divides into tibial
and common peroneal nerves roughly halfway down the posterior thigh. The tibial
component serves to innervate the hamstring muscles and the hamstring part of the
adductor magnus. The other part of adductor magnus, along with the other adductor
muscles (brevis, longus, and gracilis), is supplied by the anterior branch of the obturator
nerve. The femoral nerve supplies the quadriceps muscles and the sartorius and gives
off anterior cutaneous branches and the saphenous nerve from its posterior division.
The saphenous nerve traverses the Hunter canal with the femoral vessels and emerges
to provide cutaneous innervation to the medial leg and foot. The saphenous nerve is a
sensory branch of the femoral nerve and typically divides into an infrapatellar branch
and a sartorial branch. The infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve wraps
anteromedially between the sartorius muscle and the medial capsule and may be
injured during medial approaches to the knee. The sartorial branch of the saphenous
nerve descends with the great saphenous vein to the medial foot171-173 (Figure 28).

Golgi-like receptors also are believed to have a proprioceptive role.101
